79d2a3f00b8597ed: KUALA LUMPUR: The police action film Chelot continues to heat up cinemas and has now raked in a box office collection of RM14 million after 14 days of screening.
This success is not just a statistical figure but a manifestation of the strong support from local film fans who continue to back homegrown movies.
"Thank you for the unwavering support and for continuing to choose Chelot as your movie of choice," said the production team in a statement today.
Combining thrilling action elements with a story full of twists, this film directed by Adrian Teh proves that local movies continue to be a hit with cinemagoers.
"The production team urges audiences nationwide to continue flooding cinemas to experience this large-scale cinematic adventure with family and friends."

Primeworks Studios, as the marketing partner for the film, also invited fans of the movie to keep up with the latest updates and share the excitement through the official hashtag #CHELOT on various social media platforms.
546a879b228682bd: KUALA LUMPUR: George Kent (Malaysia) Bhd is strengthening its technology footprint through a collaboration between its wholly-owned GK SuperTech Sdn Bhd and Shandong Extreme Vision Technology Co Ltd.
The latter is a Hong Kong-listed artificial intelligence (AI) technology company.
The collaboration gives GK SuperTech exclusive rights to rebrand, market, distribute and sell Extreme Vision's AI algorithms and large models in Malaysia and Singapore.
The companies will also work together to deploy enterprise-level AI solutions and pursue opportunities across the wider Asean market.
The partnership was formalised through a binding term sheet covering the commercial deployment of Extreme Vision's proprietary AI technologies and its regional market expansion.
Extreme Vision specialises in AI-powered computer vision algorithms and large models that enable machines to interpret and analyse visual data in real time.
Its technologies are used in areas including smart cities, smart manufacturing, industrial automation, infrastructure monitoring and public safety.
As part of the collaboration, George Kent's manufacturing plant in Puchong, Selangor will serve as a pilot site for implementing Vision AI.
The facility will showcase the application of advanced AI technologies in a manufacturing environment, aiming to establish a benchmark for smart manufacturing.
George Kent executive chairman Tan Sri Tan Kay Hock said the collaboration marked a significant step in the group's expansion into Agentic AI technology.
"This collaboration provides GK SuperTech with a clear pathway to bring advanced AI solutions to Malaysia and Singapore, while creating opportunities for further growth across Asean," he said.
He said the collaboration also supported the objectives of Malaysia's National AI Action Plan 2026-2030 to accelerate AI adoption across industries.
f320fe01c1e737e4: MELAKA: A single mother of four was fined RM1,800 by the Ayer Keroh magistrate's court today after pleading guilty to assaulting a man at an eatery in Melaka Sentral in July.

Magistrate Sharda Shienha Mohd Suleiman imposed the sentence on Nurul Amalina Mohamad Kamal, 32, after taking into account her guilty plea, mitigation, the facts of the case and the prosecution's submission on sentencing.
Amalina was charged with voluntarily causing hurt to Mohd Zubir Maarof, 47, together with four other people who had previously been charged.
She was charged under Section 323 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34 of the same Code, which carries a maximum jail term of one year, a fine of up to RM2,000, or both, upon conviction.

Based on the facts of the case, the victim was punched and kicked by the accused while they were discussing a case, resulting in injuries to his back, head and nose, as well as pain in his right ribs that made it difficult for him to breathe.
The incident was captured on closed-circuit television (CCTV), while mobile phone recordings and witnesses also showed the accused assaulting and injuring the victim.
National Legal Aid Foundation lawyer Muhammad Izzuddin Ab Malek, in mitigation, pleaded for a minimum fine, saying that Amalina was unemployed and a single mother of four.
"She has promised not to repeat it and will try to control her emotions and allow the authorities to resolve any issues that arise," he said.

Deputy public prosecutor S. Thiviya urged the court to impose a sentence that would serve as a lesson to the accused to control her emotions better and leave investigations to the relevant authorities.
The court then fined Amalina RM1,800, in default of two months' imprisonment. She paid the fine.

Earlier, a commotion broke out outside the courtroom between members of the media and a man who attempted to prevent the accused from being photographed by grabbing and pushing the hands of a journalist and videographer.
Amalina, who appeared surprised by the large media presence, was heard asking, "Wow, there are so many of you. Am I an artist? Any questions?" as she was escorted by police.
She also asked a friend to record members of the media covering the proceedings.
9b0e0a8243a3f545: KUALA LUMPUR: The Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (Jakim) and the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas) have agreed on several measures to strengthen compliance and accountability in Malaysia's film and television industry.

Following a meeting between the two agencies today, it was agreed that the drama series Madu Atau Racun and Cela will proceed to the next stage, where a Jakim panel will evaluate the productions based on their overall storylines and content context, in line with the relevant guidelines.
Jakim and Finas, together with relevant agencies, will also hold engagement sessions with film and television industry players to discuss production procedures and guidelines for content creation.

In addition, Finas will introduce an additional condition under the Filming Certificate (SSP) to ensure every production complies with established guidelines and does not contain content that could adversely affect society.

Jakim said the measures should not be viewed as an attempt to restrict artistic freedom, but rather as an effort to ensure creativity develops responsibly while taking into account religious sensitivities, cultural values, public interests and the country's legal framework.

Jakim director-general Datuk Dr Sirajuddin Suhaimee said the department takes media content seriously because of its influence in conveying messages and shaping societal values, particularly on matters involving religion, morality and the sensitivities of the Muslim community.
"Creators, producers and industry players are urged to refer to the Guidelines for Screening Islamic Elements in Broadcast Materials when producing works involving religion and Islamic values.
"We also also welcomed the Communications Ministry's efforts through Finas to strengthen procedures and compliance relating to film and television content," he said in a statement released today.

He added Jakim remains committed to working with Finas and relevant agencies through engagement sessions and exchanges with industry players to improve understanding of the guidelines and ensure content respects religious values and the interests of society.
ae88233bb6c05079: KUALA LUMPUR: Umno must not allow political pressure from its opponents to divide the party or turn its own members into conduits for narratives built by its rivals, said Veteran Umno.
Reading out their resolutions at the 2026 Umno General Assembly, the group's committee member Datuk Adam Abd Hamid said the party must remain united in facing political pressure and attacks.
"Umno must unite in facing the political pressure, intimidation and attacks carried out by Pakatan Harapan against the party and its leaders.
"We do not defend wrongdoing, but we must defend justice, transparent legal processes and a person's right not to be punished based on perception.
"As Umno grows stronger, the attacks will become more intense. That is why party unity is our most important line of defence," he said in his debate.
Adam said Umno should also lead efforts to realign Malay-Muslim political strength based on the Federal Constitution, the interests of the people and national stability.
He said such a realignment should not be based on hostility towards other races, but on consolidating political strength without compromising justice or the prosperity of a multiracial society.
Prolonged divisions, he said, will only weaken Malay bargaining power and create room for others to determine the country's political agenda.
"Umno must be the leader, not merely a complement, in shaping Malay political power," it said.
On Umno's relationship with Perikatan Nasional (PN), he called for strategic understanding and negotiations to avoid clashes that could split the Malay-Muslim vote.
He said cooperation with PN must be based on sincerity, mutual respect and recognition of Umno's strength and shared interests.
"On our relationship with PN, particularly Pas, I ask that we approach it through proper negotiations.

"Do not look only at the question of power. If we focus solely on power, eventually we will fight because we want the prime minister's post, and they want the prime minister's post. We want to retain our seats, and they will want to retain theirs. Unity cannot last long that way," he said.
Instead, he said both sides should focus on areas where cooperation could benefit the Malay community, particularly economic issues and food security.
He said through Umno's experience with PH, it showed that cooperation without sincerity, mutual respect and reciprocity will only weaken Umno's identity and position.
"PH cannot be regarded as a truly trustworthy partner as long as attacks, pressure and efforts to discredit Umno continue," he said.
He also called for veterans to be formally included in Umno's election machinery at national, state, division, state constituency and polling district levels.
Adam said the veterans' experience, community networks and relationships with traditional voters could complement technology-driven campaigning.
He further called for veterans to strengthen ties with non-governmental organisations, professional bodies, retirees' associations and community groups to rebuild public confidence in Umno.

Another 47 areas nationwide recorded moderate API readings.
In Sabah, moderate readings were recorded in Kimanis at 96, Politeknik Kota Kinabalu (94), Kota Kinabalu (91), Keningau (63) and Sandakan (58).
Labuan recorded a moderate reading of 97, while Kapit (95) and Limbang (80) in Sarawak also remained in the moderate category.
In Johor, Larkin recorded a reading of 95, followed by Kota Tinggi (93), Segamat (91), Tangkak (87), Kluang (86) and Pengerang (85).

fa59e507404e41e2: KUALA LUMPUR: PTT Synergy Group Bhd subsidiary PTT Logistics Hub 3 Sdn Bhd is buying a plot of freehold land in Seberang Perai Selatan, Penang for RM62.53 million.
In its filing with Bursa Malaysia, the company said PTT Logistics signed a sale and purchase agreement (SPA) with Lee Mooi Khean for the acquisition.
The land will be held as an investment property, with potential for future development, aligning with the company's business expansion plans.
"The proposed acquisition is a strategic investment undertaken in line with the company's long-term growth and expansion objectives.

"By securing the land for future development and operational requirements, the proposed acquisition is expected to strengthen the company's asset base and facilitate the continued growth and expansion of its business over the medium to long term," it said.

PTT Synergy said the price was determined on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, after considering the acquisition's rationale and prospects, as well as indicative asking prices for comparable land in the surrounding area.
The RM62.53 million will be settled entirely in cash, funded through a combination of internally generated funds and bank borrowings.
PTT Synergy expects to complete the acquisition in the first quarter of 2027.
50ee245505d9fd97: KUALA LUMPUR: To fulfil the dream of their adopted child, 8-year-old Nur Tiara Zinnirah, comedian Achey is determined to continue in vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment for the second time with his wife, Nor Hasanah Yahaya or Anne.
Achey, 40, or Mohd Nasir Hamzah, said the decision was made after seeing Tiara increasingly show interest in children and often expressing a desire to have a sibling.
"Wherever Tiara goes, if she sees a child, she'll carry him or her. She usually carries my friends' kids. She also says she wants to meet my friends' children," he told Berita Harian yesterday.
Achey's wife Anne is currently resting at home following her second IVF treatment, which began on Sept 5.
"I've already made the decision to do it again this year with my wife. After failing the first time, this time we went to the Alhaya Fertility Centre and met Dr. Haris Hamzah.
"Dr. Haris is one of the first people to successfully do IVF in Malaysia," he said.
"This IVF process was more detailed and longer, so we went through it calmly.
"Whether it succeeds or not, it is in God's hands," he said.
Achey praised Anne for her courage, as she was willing to go through IVF again to have a child.
"IVF is painful. The process is not as easy as people think," he said.
"Among the changes Anne experienced during this treatment was rising body temperature. This made her feel hot even in an air-conditioned room."
In December 2022, Achey's wife underwent IVF treatment but was unsuccessful.
Achey and Anne were married in 2011 and adopted Tiara as their child in 2018.

25737c41e2a68b8b: KUALA LUMPUR: Umno grassroots are unlikely to reject closer cooperation with Pas if it benefits the rakyat, said a Melaka Umno leader.

Duyong assemblyman Datuk Mohd Noor Helmy Abdul Halem, who is also a deputy Melaka state executive councillor, said any potential cooperation between the two parties must be built around common ground without either side compromising its core principles.
He said both parties had several fundamental areas in common, including the rights of Malays and Bumiputera, the institution of the Malay Rulers and the sovereignty of Islam.
"Previously, Umno was on one straight line and Pas was on another. Both sides need to move slightly towards each other without compromising their principles.
"They need to find a point of convergence, and that is where a bigger joint effort can take shape," he said when met today at the 2026 Umno General Assembly here.
However, Noor Helmy said it was too early to determine whether such cooperation would translate into a formal political pact ahead of the 16th General Election (GE16).
He said Malaysia's political landscape was highly dynamic and the most suitable arrangement could differ from one state to another.
Political cooperation, he said, should therefore not be viewed solely through the lens of a national arrangement, particularly given the differing political strengths and dynamics across states.
He added that a Pas-led government might be acceptable in states such as Kelantan, Kedah, Perlis and Terengganu, but Melaka had a different political landscape.
"Johor has its own formula, Negri Sembilan has its own formula and Melaka has its own. We do not yet know which formula will be the most suitable for GE16," he said.
"As long as there is cooperation, it is not necessarily about who becomes the chief minister. What matters is how it is arranged so that everyone feels comfortable," he added.

His remarks came amid renewed discussion at the assembly on Malay unity and the possibility of closer ties between Umno and Pas, with the party leadership stressing the importance of strengthening Umno while remaining open to cooperation with other Malay-based parties.
Noor Helmy also said any cooperation should not weaken Umno's ability to stand independently.
"Political cooperation is a political strategy. A coalition is a bonus. Umno must be prepared to stand on its own feet, regardless of whether there is a coalition," he said.

817e8bf3000df90d: PETALING JAYA: DAP legal bureau chairman Ramkarpal Singh has rejected PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang’s call for non-Muslims to be restricted to Cabinet portfolios that do not involve policy formulation.
A former deputy law minister, Ramkarpal said Hadi’s remarks were unconstitutional and struck at the principles of multiculturalism and racial diversity underpinning Malaysian society.

He said he agreed with the Malaysian Consultative Council of Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Sikhism and Taoism (MCCBCHST), which today described Hadi’s remarks as an infringement of the basic structure of the Federal Constitution.
The Bukit Gelugor MP also cited Hadi’s remarks in 2018 that PAS would establish two Cabinets if it came to power - one for Muslims and another for non-Muslims.
He said such an arrangement would contravene Article 43 of the Federal Constitution, which provides for the formation of a single Cabinet.
“Article 43 makes no mention of the division of the Cabinet along racial and religious lines,” he said in a statement.
“This further suggests that it was never the intention of the forefathers of the nation that ministerial positions be divided into categories based on race and religion.”
Ramkarpal said all citizens, regardless of race or religion, were entitled to be considered for ministerial positions, in line with the principle of equality before the law under Article 8.
He said the power to appoint ministers rested with the prime minister, but Malaysia’s Cabinet had been multiracial since independence.
“There is absolutely no reason for that to change,” he said.
Ramkarpal described Hadi’s remarks as divisive and said they should be rejected as they undermined the power-sharing model that had been practised in Malaysia.

He said DAP rejects Hadi’s remarks and will always strive to ensure that multiculturalism and multiracialism remain hallmarks in all aspects of Malaysian life, including in the composition of the Cabinet.

Ramkarpal also called on non-Muslim parties in Perikatan Nasional, particularly Gerakan, to publicly state their position on Hadi’s remarks, saying the issue was in the public interest and could affect the country’s future direction.
He urged Umno and other Barisan Nasional parties, particularly MCA and MIC, to state whether they agreed with Hadi, given the recent cooperation and discussions between BN and PAS.

Hadi said last week that non-Muslims could serve as ministers, but their roles should be limited to portfolios responsible for implementing government policies, while Muslims would be tasked with formulating them.
Speaking at the conclusion of PAS’s4 72nd muktamar in Kota Bharu, he cited the works and forestry ministries as examples of portfolios that could be held by non-Muslims.
23515fd395e53d65: SEPTEMBER 11 — The world is increasingly trapped between two narrow bodies of water: the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz.
Neither is large on a map.
Yet both have become disproportionately important to the functioning of the international economy.
If instability around them deepens simultaneously, the consequences will not remain confined to West Asia.
They will travel through energy markets, shipping routes, insurance premiums, inflation and eventually the everyday cost of living across Asia and Asean.
The latest fighting in Yemen therefore deserves much more attention than it has received.
The Houthi movement is seeking to consolidate its position along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

Its advance towards the strategic port of Mocha raises the possibility of stronger Houthi influence near Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.
This cannot be viewed merely as another chapter in Yemen’s long civil war.
It changes the strategic geography of the Arabian Peninsula.

To the east lies the Strait of Hormuz, where the continuing confrontation involving Iran has already demonstrated how vulnerable the international economy becomes when freedom of navigation through a maritime chokepoint can no longer be taken for granted.
To the southwest lies Bab el-Mandeb. Between them sits the Arabian Peninsula, including Saudi Arabia and some of the world’s most important oil and gas infrastructure.
This is beginning to resemble a geopolitical pincer.
The significance does not depend on Iran controlling Hormuz completely or the Houthis physically closing Bab el-Mandeb.
Indeed, framing the problem in terms of absolute control can obscure the more important strategic reality.
Neither chokepoints has to be completely closed to inflict enormous economic damage.
Commercial shipping depends upon predictability.
Insurance depends upon calculable risks. Energy markets depend heavily upon expectations.
A handful of missiles, drones or attacks on commercial vessels can therefore produce consequences vastly disproportionate to the cost of launching them.
Shipping companies reroute vessels. Insurance premiums increase. Delivery times lengthen.
Freight charges rise. Energy traders begin pricing geopolitical uncertainty into oil and gas.
The effects cascade through the world economy. This is asymmetric warfare applied to maritime geography.
Iran understands this extremely well. So do the Houthis.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

To the east lies the Strait of Hormuz, where the continuing confrontation involving Iran has already demonstrated how vulnerable the international economy becomes when freedom of navigation through a maritime chokepoint can no longer be taken for granted. — AFP pic
The strategic problem confronting Saudi Arabia is consequently becoming more complicated.
Riyadh has long understood the vulnerability created by dependence on Hormuz and has developed infrastructure allowing some oil exports to move westwards towards the Red Sea.
But a bypass around one chokepoint becomes less reassuring when another chokepoint becomes unstable.
That is precisely why developments around Yemen’s Red Sea coast matter.

If pressure continues around Hormuz while insecurity intensifies around Bab el-Mandeb, Saudi Arabia and the Gulf economies could find themselves confronting strategic uncertainty on two maritime fronts simultaneously.
The United States faces a similar dilemma.
American military power remains formidable.
It can strike missile batteries, radar installations, weapons depots and command centres.
Yet military superiority cannot change geography.

Nor can aircraft carriers permanently guarantee the safety of every commercial vessel passing through narrow waterways surrounded by potentially hostile forces. Especially when air craft carriers are vulnerable to the drones.
This is the uncomfortable lesson of asymmetric warfare.
A weaker actor does not necessarily have to defeat a stronger power militarily. It merely has to impose sufficient costs to alter the stronger power’s calculations.
The Houthis have already demonstrated the ability to use missiles and drones to disrupt shipping and challenge much larger military powers.
Iran possesses considerably greater capabilities.
The possibility that pressure from Iran around Hormuz could coincide with sustained Houthi pressure around Bab el-Mandeb therefore creates something larger than two separate regional crises.
It risks producing a single interconnected maritime-security crisis stretching around the Arabian Peninsula.
ASEAN cannot afford to regard this as somebody else’s problem.
Southeast Asia is geographically distant from Yemen and Iran, but economically it is intimately connected to both waterways.
Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei may possess their own hydrocarbon resources, yet their economies remain exposed to global energy prices.
Singapore is one of the world’s most important maritime, refining, financial and logistical centres.
Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam remain heavily dependent upon international trade and imported energy.
Across Asean higher shipping costs eventually become higher production costs. Higher oil prices affect transportation and electricity.
Higher insurance premiums become another invisible tax on trade.
Inflation consequently travels much further than missiles.

This is especially important when Asean economies are simultaneously attempting to manage slower global growth, supply-chain restructuring, technological competition between the United States and China and the enormous investment requirements associated with the green and digital transitions.
Another prolonged energy shock is the last thing Southeast Asia needs.
The situation therefore demands diplomacy of a scale commensurate with the geography.
The Strait of Hormuz must be returned to normal commercial navigation.
The Yemeni conflict must not be allowed to transform Bab el-Mandeb into another permanent theatre of maritime confrontation.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have reasons to avoid returning to the devastating patterns of their earlier conflict.
Iran, too, ultimately requires functioning energy markets.

A permanently destabilised Strait of Hormuz may provide temporary strategic leverage, but it cannot provide Iran with the sustained oil revenues and economic normalisation that the country ultimately needs.
Washington should understand the same paradox. Military pressure can deter certain actions.
It cannot indefinitely substitute for diplomacy.
The world therefore needs to resist becoming trapped by the strategic logic now forming around the Arabian Peninsula.
There is a route out, but it requires simultaneous diplomatic engagement with the crises affecting Yemen, the Red Sea, Iran and Hormuz rather than treating each as an isolated security problem.
The alternative is dangerous.
A world economy already struggling with geopolitical fragmentation could find two of its most important maritime arteries under pressure at the same time.
Bab el-Mandeb in the west. Hormuz in the east.
The Arabian Peninsula caught between them.
And the rest of the world paying the bill. Asean may be thousands of kilometres away from both waterways, but geography no longer provides economic insulation.
When the Red Sea becomes unstable and the Strait of Hormuz remains under pressure, Southeast Asia will be affected by the perpetual chaos in West Asia.
* Phar Kim Beng is a professor of Asean Studies, and director at the Institute of International and Asean Studies, International Islamic University Malaysia.

50f2525358d75108: KATHMANDU: The reconstruction bill after deadly floods sparked by a glacial mountain collapse that hit Nepal last month would amount to US$4.78 billion, the foreign ministry said on Friday.
The tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris on Aug 26, which began on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people and left some 5,600 missing.
"The total estimated requirement for reconstruction is approximately US$4.78 billion," Nepali foreign ministry spokesman Lok Bahadur Chhetri told reporters.

"Of this, approximately US$57.67 million is estimated to be required for short-term reconstruction and recovery over the next six months, while approximately US$4.71 billion is required for longer-term reconstruction."
Nepal's leaders say the Himalayan country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, contributes a fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions compared to industrialised nations.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

"Given the scale and extent of the damage, the government is also undertaking a comprehensive post-disaster needs assessment to determine the full extent of loss and damage and the requirement for recovery, rebuilding and reconstruction," Chhetri said.

Rescuers in Nepal have retrieved 1,385 bodies, while around 5,130 people are missing, according to the disaster agency on Friday. In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media.

26c834d5775d4eec: KUALA LUMPUR: Bekas ketua menteri Sabah Salleh Said Keruak berkata cadangan Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim untuk menambah perwakilan Sabah dan Sarawak di Parlimen akan memulihkan keseimbangan penting yang wujud ketika Malaysia dibentuk.

bd398b07bcc5b897: KOTA KINABALU, Sept 11 — A total of RM1.52 billion has been allocated for 8,069 small-scale projects and People’s Facility Initiatives (IKR) nationwide since 2023, with Sabah receiving the largest share at RM582.29 million for 2,301 projects.

dd49f02709de3786: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 11 — The Alor Setar High Court has dismissed an application by GISB Holdings Sdn Bhd (GISBH) and its Chief Executive Officer, Nasiruddin Mohd Ali, for leave to initiate judicial review proceedings to challenge a state fatwa issued against them last year.

The fatwa, issued by the Kedah State Fatwa Committee on February 12 last year, ruled that the beliefs, teachings, tenets and practices of GISBH members and followers were deviant and contrary to Islamic teachings.

The committee also ruled that any Muslim who acted in contravention of the fatwa committed an offence under the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment (Kedah Darul Aman) 2014 and was liable to legal action under the laws in force in Kedah.

Judge Evawani Farisyta Mohammad dismissed the application by GISBH and Nasiruddin after allowing the Attorney General’s objection to their application for leave to commence judicial review proceedings.

In the grounds of judgment dated September 7, which was uploaded on the judiciary’s website, the judge said the contents of the fatwa were based on Syariah law and therefore fell within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Syariah Court, meaning that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to determine the matter.
“…this court, regarding the reliefs sought by the applicants (GISBH and Nasiruddin), is essentially being asked to review the content or substance of the fatwa and to quash it,” she said.
Judge Evawani also said the fatwa referred to individuals involved with GISBH rather than GISBH as a corporate entity.

She noted that the fatwa was issued pursuant to the prerogative powers of the Sultan of Kedah and was therefore a decision that was non-justiciable and could not be challenged through judicial review.
In their application for leave, GISBH and Nasiruddin had sought an order of certiorari to quash the decision made by the respondents through the issuance of the fatwa.
The applicants named the Kedah State Fatwa Committee, Kedah State Islamic Religious Council and Mufti of Kedah as respondents.

Nasiruddin and GISBH claimed that the fatwa had adversely affected their operations and reputation, as well as those of individuals associated with them, and had resulted in them being perceived as followers of deviant teachings.

The Attorney General objected to the application on the grounds that the fatwa was not subject to judicial review or adjudication, as it constituted an exercise of the Ruler’s prerogative powers. — Bernama
e6a3b33694d18c8b: NEW DELHI: Malaysia should join the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) to share its expertise in managing natural disasters, says its director-general Amit Prothi.
CDRI director-general Amit Prothi said Malaysia, as an Asean member, had extensive experience in dealing with disasters including landslides, tsunamis and major earthquakes.

He said the coalition was keen to strengthen cooperation with Asean countries and regional organisations, including the Asean Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management (AHA Centre) in Indonesia.
"Many countries in Asean have been working on the disaster-resilient infrastructure agenda for a long time, and we very much want to build partnerships with them.
"Vietnam is already a member, while the Philippines will become a member tomorrow. So, I hope more countries from Asean will join us," he said.
Prothi was speaking during a briefing for an international media delegation hosted by India's External Affairs Ministry in New Delhi and Mumbai today.
The visit was organised as part of the Indian government's initiatives ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit, which will be held in New Delhi this weekend.
Malaysia is participating in the BRICS Leaders' Summit as a BRICS partner country.
The CDRI was initiated by the Indian government and formally launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the United Nations Climate Action Summit in New York in September 2019.
The coalition focuses on strengthening infrastructure such as roads, bridges, hospitals, water supply systems and electricity grids to withstand the impact of climate change and natural disasters.

Its work covers risks including floods, earthquakes, tsunamis and landslides, while also providing a platform for member countries to exchange technology, research findings, technical standards and post-disaster recovery practices.
It also helps developing countries and highly vulnerable areas, including small island nations, gain access to international financing and expertise to upgrade infrastructure following disasters.
Prothi said Malaysia would be a valuable addition to the coalition given its experience in managing climate-related risks.
"At the same time, the risk of natural disasters is increasing in every country. In Malaysia, for example, floods are a major problem.
"If you look at major urban areas such as Kuala Lumpur and Melaka, flooding is an issue. Extreme heat is also beginning to pose a challenge.
"For me, it would be very good if Malaysia joined us. The expertise and experience you have can be shared with other countries and also brought back to benefit your own country," he said.
Prothi said Asean's collective experience in disaster management could also benefit other countries facing similar challenges.
He cited Colombia, which recently experienced a major earthquake and sought CDRI's advice on rebuilding damaged infrastructure.
"That kind of experience is available in countries such as Indonesia and the Philippines," he said.

9cac58c08513c483: KUALA LUMPUR: The Umno Overseas Club has proposed setting up a community emergency response network to help Malaysian diplomatic missions assist citizens abroad during crises.

Newcastle Umno Overseas Club president Muhammad Amir Ikram Mohd Fadil said the network could link Malaysian communities abroad with embassies and consulates to help identify citizens who needed urgent assistance.
He said the proposal was not intended to take over the role of Malaysian diplomatic missions, but to serve as a link between the missions and communities on the ground.
"We do not want to take over the duties of the embassy. We want to be a link between the embassy and the community on the ground.

"When an emergency happens, we want to quickly identify who needs help, who has young children and who has been cut off from food supplies," he said while debating the Umno president's policy speech at the 2026 Umno General Assembly.
Amir said Malaysian communities abroad were often better placed to identify the immediate needs of fellow Malaysians during emergencies because they were already present in affected areas.
He said a coordinated network would allow communities to respond more quickly while diplomatic missions handled official assistance and consular matters.
"Technology can tell us where we are. The embassy can provide assistance. But the community ensures that no one is left behind," he said.
He said Malaysians living overseas could face a range of unexpected emergencies, including geopolitical conflicts, airspace closures, cancelled flights and natural disasters.
"The world today is uncertain. Geopolitical conflicts can erupt within hours. Airspace can be closed, flights can be cancelled and natural disasters can happen," he said.
He also highlighted concerns over food supply disruptions and growing anti-Islam sentiment in some parts of the world as additional challenges faced by Malaysians abroad.

Amir said the government had already introduced measures such as the e-Konsular system, which allowed Malaysians overseas to register their whereabouts and helped facilitate assistance during emergencies.
He said the proposed community network could complement existing government systems by providing a stronger grassroots response.
He also called for Malaysian community facilities abroad, including Malaysia Halls, to be maintained and modernised as part of the country's support network for Malaysians overseas.
Amir said the Umno Overseas Club could play a greater role in connecting Malaysian communities with government agencies and ensuring that citizens abroad had avenues to seek assistance when needed.
"We must ensure that those who are far from home are not left to face these situations alone," he said.
8132eece084c3bbe: NOT all fat is the same.
When it comes to obesity or being overweight, the most obvious thing that people focus on is what they see in the mirror or the number on the scale.
However, health experts are increasingly emphasising that where fat is stored can matter as much as how much a person weighs.
This is particularly relevant in Malaysia, where abdominal obesity remains an important health concern.
The 2023 National Health and Morbidity Survey found that 54.5 per cent of Malaysian adults had abdominal obesity based on waist circumference criteria, up from 45.4 per cent in 2011.
Understanding abdominal fat is important because a person's weight or Body Mass Index (BMI) alone does not provide a complete picture of metabolic health and not all body fat behaves in the same way.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) defines obesity as abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that presents a risk to health.
It goes beyond the number on the scale, so we need a more holistic approach to assess obesity, says Premier Clinic senior aesthetic doctor Dr Foo Wing Jian.
UNDERSTANDING FAT
Subcutaneous fat is stored beneath the skin and is the type of fat that is generally visible or can be felt around areas such as the abdomen, hips and thighs, explains Dr Foo.

Visceral fat, on the other hand, is stored deeper inside the abdominal cavity around internal organs. This distinction matters because excess visceral fat is associated with a range of metabolic health risks, including insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and chronic inflammation.
Importantly, an individual does not necessarily need to appear severely overweight to have increased abdominal or visceral fat.
This means relying exclusively on body weight or appearance may give people a false sense of reassurance about their health.
"Many people think that if their weight is not extremely high, there is no reason to be concerned. But weight alone does not tell the whole story," Dr Foo says.

Abdominal obesity can be an important warning sign of underlying metabolic risk. This is why it is important to look beyond kilogrammes lost and consider factors such as waist circumference, body composition, medical history and metabolic health when assessing an individual's weight management needs.
DISPELLING MYTHS
Besides the "thin is healthy" belief, another common misconception is that losing weight is simply a matter of willpower.
Dr Foo says the body has sophisticated biological mechanisms that regulate hunger, satiety, energy intake and body weight.
During weight loss, changes in appetite and other physiological processes can make it difficult for some individuals to maintain their initial weight loss over the long term.

This is one reason why repeated cycles of dieting and weight regain can occur. While nutrition, physical activity, sleep and behavioural changes remain important foundations of healthy weight management, some individuals may require additional medical support.

This has contributed to the growing role of medical weight management, where healthcare professionals assess an individual's health and weight-related risks before determining whether treatment may be appropriate.
Medical weight management is now being explored as an option for people with obesity.

Such treatments help patients experience reduced appetite and increased feelings of fullness, which can support a reduction in food intake and, alongside appropriate lifestyle measures, meaningful weight loss.
This represents an important shift from the traditional perception that weight loss is simply about eating less and exercising more.

"Medications are changing the way we think about obesity because they address some of the biological pathways involved in appetite and metabolism. For certain patients, this treatment can provide an additional tool alongside nutrition, physical activity and behavioural changes."
However, Dr Foo cautions that prescription treatment should only be used following proper medical assessment and under the supervision of a qualified healthcare professional.
Furthermore, not everyone who wants to lose weight is necessarily an appropriate candidate for prescription weight-management medication.

Dr Foo says treatment decisions should take into consideration factors such as BMI, waist circumference, existing medical conditions, medications, metabolic health, lifestyle and individual treatment goals.
As weight-related health concerns continue to affect Malaysians, greater public understanding is needed to move the conversation beyond appearance and short-term dieting, he adds.

Recognising the difference between visible body fat and visceral fat, understanding the biological factors that influence weight and knowing when medical intervention may be appropriate can empower people to make more informed health decisions.
Medical weight management treatments represent an evolving area of healthcare, but their role is not to replace healthy lifestyle habits or promote rapid cosmetic weight loss.
The aim is to provide evidence-based medical support for individuals who may require more than lifestyle intervention alone.
FAT FACTS
*Not all health risks are visible on the weighing scale.
*The location of body fat matters.
*Weight loss should not be viewed only in terms of kilograms, but also in improvements to body composition and metabolic health.
*A person does not necessarily have to appear severely overweight to have metabolic risk factors.
*Excess weight is not just an appearance issue.
*Weight management is not simply a matter of willpower.

b36407902b801f86: LONDON: British MPs were on Friday set to vote again on an assisted dying bill as protesters both for and against the proposed legislation gathered outside parliament.
The legislation was passed in a landmark vote in the lower house of parliament last year before being struck down in the unelected upper house.
The controversial legislation to legalise assisted dying has had a long and emotional passage through parliament, with lawmakers on both sides of the debate making impassioned speeches.
The bill would allow adults in England and Wales who have been given less than six months to live and can clearly express a wish to die to opt for euthanasia.
They would need the approval of two doctors and an expert panel to make the decision.
It passed in a historic vote in the House of Commons last June, but was scuppered by more than 1,200 amendments in the House of Lords, which was accused of obstructing and delaying the legislation.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was reintroduced by an MP from the ruling Labour party in the new parliamentary session.
If it passes at this stage, it will go forward for further debate, potential amendments and a final vote before going on to the Lords.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will sit out the vote so as to not "unduly influence the debate".
Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has relaunched his years-long push to improve social care for the elderly and vulnerable, and has supported prioritising palliative care.
Lauren Edwards, the MP who brought back the bill, urged lawmakers to pass it again and send it back to the House of Lords, "so that they can finish what they started".
aee30439a79b692f: KUALA LUMPUR: Actor Zul Ariffin is more cautious in performing scenes in dramas following legal action for appearing in a sensitive scene four years ago.
According to Zul, 40, the past experience taught him not to blindly follow every instruction and drama script.
"I've been through that, so I won't put myself in a position where I just nod to whatever they tell me to do in the script.
"As actors, we need to understand the meaning of collaboration. If not, we'll end up being fools.
"If something happens, they'll throw you under the bus. That's not good.
"I learnt this the hard way, and that's why I have to be careful," he told Harian Metro yesterday.
Zul admitted: "I want to close that chapter and move on."
When asked for his opinion on local drama Madu Atau Racun that had to be re-edited following allegations of sensitive scenes, Zul welcomed the move.
"It's good if there's action. But there were many times when nothing was done," he shared.
Commenting on netizens who enjoy picking on drama scenes on social media, Zul said that the platform wasn't capable of solving problems.
"I don't know what's going on these days, everyone wants to report things on social media. Social media isn't an authority or an association, it's just a place for people to complain."
Zul urged the public to use proper channels to resolve issues concerning drama scenes.
"Social media is for people to make money, it's not a place to complain," he said.
Zul added that he chose to keep quiet rather than complain on social media because he was focused on his acting career.
Zul sparked controversy in 2022 when he uploaded a clip from his drama series Perempuan Itu which drew criticism from many.
Zul was fined RM30,000 after pleading guilty at the Sepang Sessions Court on Oct 4, 2022, for uploading sensitive content on social media in March that year.

d63c428ceef0eb0a: KUALA LUMPUR: Former Sabah chief minister Salleh Said Keruak says Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s proposal to increase parliamentary representation for Sabah and Sarawak will restore an important balance that existed when Malaysia was formed.
Salleh said the two Bornean states should collectively hold at least one-third of the seats in Parliament, consistent with the safeguards and spirit surrounding the formation of the federation.
The Sabah Umno treasurer said Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore had collectively provided an important parliamentary balance when Malaysia was formed in 1963.
Malaya was allocated 105 of the 160 seats in the Dewan Rakyat - representing 65% of the voting power in the House - with Sarawak holding 24 seats, Sabah 16, and Singapore 15.

This denied Malaya the two-thirds majority required to amend the Federal Constitution. However, after Singapore's departure, its 15 seats were not redistributed to Sabah and Sarawak, causing the two states to lose their veto power.

“This is not simply about giving Sabah and Sarawak a few additional seats. It is about restoring an important balance associated with the original formation of Malaysia," he said in a statement today.
“Restoring the one-third parliamentary balance is not about weakening Malaysia. It is about strengthening the federal partnership and respecting the foundations upon which Malaysia was formed.”

Sabah (25 seats) and Sarawak (31 seats) currently hold a combined total of 56 parliamentary seats (25.2%) out of the 222 seats in the Dewan Rakyat. This is 18 seats shy of achieving one-third representatiion.
Earlier today, Anwar said the Federal Constitution would be amended to allow for an increase in parliamentary seats for the two states in accordance with the Malaysia Agreement 1963.
Anwar said the increase is necessary to ensure the two states have greater representation in Parliament.
He also said while the possibility of more parliamentary seats in Peninsular Malaysia cannot be ruled out, it must not undermine the need to increase the representation of Sabah and Sarawak.
cc78dcf2d03dfe78: KUALA LUMPUR: Flash floods at Zoo Negara two days ago were triggered by persistent heavy rain that caused water from Sungai Pandan and Sungai Kemensah in Hulu Klang to converge and overflow.

"That is the hippo area, and they naturally like being submerged in water, so they had no problems," he said.

4169a28bda9f7f94: SHAH ALAM: Driven by grief after losing her youngest child, a former beautician turned traditional healer fell deeper into delusion, eventually believing her deceased child had possessed her to grant her spiritual healing powers.
That mental collapse culminated on a July evening in 2022 inside an Ampang home, when a ritual meant to "exorcise a ghost" ended in a brutal killing.
The High Court acquitted 55-year-old Che Hong Chiew of murdering her client, 41-year-old Lim Sin Hue, after ruling that Che was of unsound mind during the violent episode.
Judicial Commissioner Suriyati Hasimah Mohd Hashim found that Che was suffering from schizophrenia at the time, leaving her unable to understand the nature or consequences of her actions.
Instead of sentencing Che to death or jail, the court ordered her to be detained at Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta in Perak at the pleasure of the Sultan of Selangor.
The prosecution has appealed against the ruling.
The tragic encounter began when Lim, who suffered from severe abdominal pain and believed that a baby was inside her stomach, was introduced to Che by a friend.
Lim agreed to undergo a week-long Buddhist healing ritual at Che's residence in Pandan Perdana, Ampang.
However, when Lim and her mother went to Che's house on July 27, 2022, the horror began to unfold.
Locked inside the home to prevent "disruption," Lim's mother looked on as Che lay on top of her daughter, punching her chest, biting her private parts, and stomping on her abdomen.
As she recited mantras, Che pressed a hot, steaming bowl directly against Lim's neck and mouth.
When Lim's mother tried to intervene, Che warned her to stay back, insisting the violent beatings were necessary to drive out a "demonic disturbance" residing in the victim's stomach.
The intensity of the assault left Lim immobilised and unable to scream.
Sometime around 5pm, Che told Lim's mother that the 41-year-old had died, and apologised. She promised she would take care of the grieving mother for the rest of her life.
Che then washed and dressed Lim's body, claiming that her spiritual "sifu" (master) and the police were on their way.

A subsequent post-mortem examination showed that Lim had died from severe blunt force trauma, suffering multiple abrasions and bruises to her face, chest, abdomen and upper and lower limbs, as well as numerous broken ribs.
During the trial, the court heard how Che's life spiralled out of control following the death of her youngest child in an accident, which was further compounded by a 2018 divorce.
The mother of two then began spending long hours at a local temple and, over time, became convinced she could see, hear, and speak to her late child.
Around a month before the fatal incident, Che believed her child had possessed her body, granting her the ability to see spirits and cure possessed individuals.
When treating Lim using a mix of mantras, herbal massage, cupping, and gua sha, Che claimed two spirits took over her body and mind, giving her a surge of energy and strength.
She maintained that she only realised something was wrong when Lim suddenly stopped moving or breathing.

Psychiatric expert Dr. Isabel Shamini David testified that Che had schizophrenia and was actively delusional during the assault, though her condition could be stabilised through medication and psychiatric care.

In her grounds of judgment, the judicial commissioner noted that while direct and circumstantial evidence proved Lim died at Che's hands, Che's mind was profoundly fractured by years of unaddressed trauma.
"Her unstable mental state had persisted for a long time, stemming from the death of her youngest child, which led to depression and social withdrawal, compounded by a divorce," Suriyati said.
"These circumstances placed a heavy emotional strain on her, ultimately resulting in a diagnosis of schizophrenia."
"Her intention was to remove what she believed to be a ghost from Lim's stomach, rather than to kill her," she said.
The court concluded that Che truly believed she was driving a ghost from Lim's abdomen and lacked any intention or realization that her physical assault would result in death.
Deputy public prosecutor Ainul Mardiyah Mohd Ali appeared for the prosecution, while Che was represented by Datuk Geethan Ram Vincent and Jeremiah Anand.

f5569ae7e6d68488: NEW DELHI: Leaders from Russia and Iran were in India for talks on Friday, ahead of a BRICS summit dominated by conflict and economic challenges, which Chinese President Xi Jinping will also attend.
Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit that opens on Saturday, when Xi is set to arrive.

It will be Xi's first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
"China stands ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences," Beijing's foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Friday.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi's visit.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to hold talks on Friday with President Vladimir Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.

"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Modi wrote Friday, in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who arrived in New Delhi on Friday and will hold talks with Modi, said that "BRICS was established to counter unilateralism", according to Tehran's IRNA news agency.
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement -- the expansion of BRICS -- today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
Pezeshkian's participation -- his first visit to India as Iranian president -- will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.

"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".
cc7328d7e9b05613: KUALA LUMPUR: Perwakilan Umno Perak memberi peringatan bahawa kerjasama dengan PAS tidak boleh mengorbankan kelangsungan hidup Umno.

6274d53c6c1a4830: KUALA LUMPUR: The failure of previous attempts to unite Malay-based parties was mainly because of disagreements over seat allocations, says Tampin Umno chief Isam Isa.
Debating the Umno president's policy speech at the general assembly here today, Isam said seat negotiations were difficult as the strengths of Umno and PAS varied from state to state.
“As a party man, I admit that this is difficult and not easy to accept because there are states where Umno is strong and there are also states where PAS is strong,” he said.

He said Negeri Sembilan Umno was willing to sacrifice winnable seats such as Gemas, Klawang and Sikamat in the interest of greater Malay political unity, despite having already identified their potential candidates.
“An understanding will not happen if we take all the seats and there is no give and take,” he said.
He said the move had paid off, with Umno eventually returning to lead the Negeri Sembilan government.
Isam called for Umno to remain a party built on loyalty rather than positions, saying members should remain committed even when the party is not in power.
“Umno was never built on positions. Umno was built on loyalty, sacrifice and discipline in its struggle.
"Be loyal during difficult times, endure defeat, and do not leave the party when it is not in power. This distinguishes a fighter from a passenger,” he said.
Isam said those given opportunities and entrusted with responsibilities through Umno has a moral and political obligation to remain loyal to the party.
He took aim at former Umno leaders Puad Zarkashi and Tengku Zafrul Aziz, accusing them of having treated the party like a “political transit station”.
Puad quit Umno in June, shortly before the Johor state election, after saying he would not defend the Rengit state seat.
Tengku Zafrul left Umno in May 2025 and joined PKR in August.
566f93b0239b5d80: KUALA LUMPUR: An Umno Youth delegate says the party must safeguard its political interests in any Malay-Muslim political cooperation.
Perak Umno Youth delegate Iqbal Jamaluddin said he supported Malay-Muslim unity, but stressed that any political cooperation must take Umno's interests into account.
“Yes, we need to come together in the interest of Malay-Muslim unity. But at the same time, we must not lose sight of Umno's survival,” he said at the party’s annual general assembly here.
Iqbal said Umno must avoid becoming a party that was strong only in certain states, such as Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka.
He also questioned whether Umno’s recent gains among younger voters reflected genuine support for the party or were driven by dissatisfaction with Pakatan Harapan.
“Is it because they genuinely want to vote for Umno? Or are they voting for Umno because they do not like PH?” he said.
He said Umno must work towards ensuring that voters choose the party and Barisan Nasional on their own merits at the 16th general election.
“By GE16, people should vote for BN because they support Umno and BN, not because they dislike PH,” he said.
Iqbal said Umno must also offer a forward-looking agenda addressing the "everyday concerns" of voters, rather than focusing solely on its traditional emphasis on Islam and Malay interests.
Apart from the cost of living and job opportunities, he said, the party should discuss topics such as technology and artificial intelligence.

5ff3564ae1d5539e: From Samirul Ariff Othman
In an earlier discussion of Balabac, I argued that Malaysia should neither overreact to military developments on the Philippine island nor dismiss them simply because relations with Manila are good.

Balabac is one of nine Philippine locations covered by the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) with the US, but it remains a military facility under Philippine control. There is little reason to suggest that the Philippines is preparing to threaten Sabah.

The larger question is whether Malaysia sufficiently understands the strategic geography taking shape immediately north of Sabah. There is another dimension to that geography. It lies beneath the sea.
The geography beneath the geography

The waters between northwest Borneo and southwest Palawan form part of a wider geological environment associated with the Baram-Balabac petroleum province. Offshore Sabah is a mature and commercially important hydrocarbon region.
West Balabac, by contrast, remains a frontier exploration area.
The two should not be treated as identical. But neither should their geological relationship be ignored.

The Baram-Balabac Basin is a recognised geological province associated with the northwest Borneo margin. Its petroleum systems have produced substantial oil and gas discoveries offshore Sabah, while geological studies indicate related structures extending northwards towards the waters southwest of Palawan.
The Philippine authorities themselves recognised this possibility.

Service Contract 59, or SC59, covers approximately 14,760 sq km west of Balabac Island. The block was awarded to PNOC Exploration Corporation in 2006 and subsequently explored with the involvement of BHP Billiton, which attracted attention partly because of its proximity to successful Malaysian deepwater discoveries.
Philippine petroleum assessments have acknowledged the possibility that West Balabac shares elements of the petroleum system found farther south.
The distinction is important. It does not mean Malaysia and the Philippines are sitting above a single proven oilfield divided by a maritime boundary.
Nor does it establish commercially recoverable reserves in West Balabac.
Geology does not respect political borders, but geological continuity is not the same thing as proven reserves.
The Malaysian side is considerably more developed.

Offshore Sabah contains producing fields, platforms, pipelines and processing infrastructure built over decades. Sabah has historically contributed a substantial proportion of Malaysia's crude-oil production. Its offshore petroleum economy is therefore not peripheral to Malaysia's national energy system.
Malikai illustrates the scale of this industry. Located 100km to 110km offshore Sabah, it is Malaysia's first tension-leg platform and an important deepwater development.
Shell’s 2026 decision to proceed with Malikai Phase 3 will add four producing wells, with production expected to rise from approximately 25,000 barrels per day to around 40,000 barrels per day.
Sabah is also seeking a larger role in the petroleum value chain through greater local participation, technical capability and ownership of producing assets.

The political economy is consequently changing. The question is no longer simply how much petroleum is extracted from Sabah, but how much ownership, capability, employment and economic value Sabah retains from it.
The waters immediately south of Balabac therefore matter economically to Malaysia, independent of any military consideration.
Oil does not explain EDCA
It would be a mistake to draw a straight line from petroleum geology to military developments on Balabac.

There is no persuasive public evidence that Philippine military expansion, or US access under EDCA, is intended to secure West Balabac’s petroleum resources, threaten Malaysian offshore installations or position US forces around Sabah’s oilfields.

The publicly stated strategic logic is more straightforward. The Philippines is strengthening territorial defence and maritime-domain awareness while confronting growing pressure in the South China Sea. Its alliance with the US is central to that strategy.
Malaysia should therefore avoid seeing conspiracies when strategic geography provides a simpler explanation.
Balabac occupies an unusually consequential location. Immediately to its south lies Sabah and an extensive Malaysian offshore petroleum economy.

To its west lies the South China Sea. Around West Balabac lies an underexplored Philippine petroleum frontier. Across the wider region run maritime routes connecting the South China Sea, the Sulu Sea and the waters surrounding northern Borneo.
Military geography, maritime geography and energy geography overlap.
The appropriate Malaysian response is therefore neither protest nor complacency, but awareness.

Malaysia and the Philippines have many common interests. Both face illegal fishing, smuggling, piracy, kidnapping and other transnational threats around the Sulu and Celebes seas. Both have an interest in preventing increasingly crowded maritime spaces from becoming increasingly dangerous ones.
Defence engagement, maritime dialogue and transparency should therefore accompany developments around Balabac.
The energy dimension provides another reason for cooperation.
SC59 remains an exploration frontier. But exploration frontiers can change. A significant commercial discovery in West Balabac would alter the economic geography of the area.

Platforms, drilling vessels, subsea installations and support vessels could eventually join military, coastguard, fishing and commercial traffic. Maritime-domain awareness would then become not merely a defence requirement but an economic-security requirement.
Malaysia has every reason to understand that environment before circumstances compel it to do so.
3 maps, 1 problem

A political map shows Malaysia ending at one line and the Philippines beginning on the other. A geological map tells a different story. Sedimentary basins continue beneath political boundaries. Petroleum systems follow geology rather than sovereignty.

A maritime map reveals another reality. Shipping routes, fishing grounds and security challenges connect waters that political borders divide. To be strategic we must be capable of reading all three maps simultaneously.

None of this makes Balabac a threat to Malaysia. Nor should American access to Philippine facilities automatically be interpreted as hostile to Malaysian interests. The Philippines is entitled to make its own defence arrangements, just as Malaysia is entitled to assess their implications.
Good foreign policy distinguishes capability from intention, geography from sovereignty, and possibility from evidence.

Malaysia should therefore maintain close communication with Manila, improve maritime-domain awareness around Sabah and protect critical offshore infrastructure without unnecessarily turning a manageable strategic development into a bilateral dispute.
The first lesson of Balabac was that friendship matters, diplomacy matters, but defence is insurance.
The second is equally simple: what lies beneath the sea can sometimes matter as much as what is built on shore.
Samirul Ariff Othman is a lecturer, international relations analyst and senior consultant. He is also an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
3184e2b8e57a290f: KUALA LUMPUR: Bursa Malaysia ended the week sharply lower on Friday, tracking a regional sell-off as persistently high crude oil prices weighed on sentiment, an analyst said.

62e0eca8c6bb0715: JAKARTA, Sept 11 — Indonesian authorities have detained 30 Malaysians suspected of running online scam activities from a hotel in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, allegedly targeting fellow Malaysians.

Pontianak Immigration Office chief Sam Fernando said the Malaysians, comprising 22 men and eight women, were detained along with a Taiwanese man at the hotel at about 11.15am on Tuesday in a joint operation with Pontianak City Police following intelligence on suspicious activities involving foreigners.
Sam said the 31 foreign nationals had used 14 rooms in the hotel for their activities.
“The targets were most likely Malaysian nationals. They were allegedly attempting to defraud Malaysian nationals,” he told a press conference on Thursday, according to a video uploaded online.
Based on the information obtained so far, Sam said there were no Indonesians among the targets.
All 31 were taken to the Pontianak Immigration Detention Centre for further questioning, with several items linked to the suspected activities also seized.

Sam said three Malaysian nationals were found to have overstayed, while there were also cases of misuse of stay permits for activities that were not in accordance with the purposes for which they were granted.
They also had not arrived together, with some entering through Pontianak airport, the Entikong land border crossing and Jakarta using various types of immigration permits, he said.
“The length of time they have been here varies. Some have been here for two months, while others for three weeks,” he said.
Sam said his office would coordinate with relevant Malaysian authorities as investigations into the case continued. — Bernama

bcbec7766bee9c37: PETALING JAYA: Persetujuan secara prinsip oleh Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim untuk menambah jumlah kerusi Parlimen bagi Sabah dan Sarawak mesti dilaksanakan, kata seorang menteri Sarawak.

Menteri Pelancongan, Industri Kreatif dan Seni Persembahan Sarawak, Abdul Karim Rahman Hamzah, berkata Putrajaya mesti memastikan cadangan itu tidak kekal sekadar hasrat, sebaliknya menghasilkan perubahan sebenar dalam perwakilan di Parlimen.
"Pandangan perdana menteri mesti disusuli dengan tindakan konkrit," kata Karim, yang juga ketua penerangan Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), menurut kenyataan.

"Usaha mesti dilakukan untuk menangani perkara ini dan akhirnya memberikan rakyat Sabah dan Sarawak harapan bahawa ini bukan sekadar pandangan perdana menteri, tetapi sesuatu yang benar-benar akan dilaksanakan."
Terdahulu, Anwar mengumumkan kerajaan secara prinsip bersetuju untuk meminda Perlembagaan bagi membolehkan penambahan wakil Parlimen dari Sabah dan Sarawak, selaras Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63).
Beliau berkata prinsip utama ialah nisbah kerusi Sabah dan Sarawak lebih tinggi, namun Putrajaya masih belum menetapkan jumlah khusus.

Karim berkata pendirian Anwar mencerminkan semangat di sebalik pembentukan Malaysia pada 1963 serta perlindungan yang dipersetujui Sabah, Sarawak dan Singapura, termasuk aturan perwakilan di Parlimen yang memberikan negeri-negeri Borneo dan Singapura kira-kira 1/3 daripada kerusi di Parlimen.

Ketika Malaysia dibentuk pada 1963, Malaya diperuntukkan 105 daripada 160 kerusi di Dewan Rakyat (mewakili 65% kuasa mengundi di Dewan), manakala Sarawak memegang 24 kerusi, Sabah 16 dan Singapura 15.

Keadaan ini menghalang Tanah Melayu daripada memperoleh majoriti 2/3 yang diperlukan untuk meminda Perlembagaan. Bagaimanapun, selepas Singapura keluar dari Malaysia, 15 kerusinya tidak diagihkan semula kepada Sabah dan Sarawak, menyebabkan negeri-negeri Borneo kehilangan kuasa veto.

Sabah (25 kerusi) dan Sarawak (31 kerusi) kini mempunyai sejumlah 56 kerusi Parlimen (25.2%) daripada 222 kerusi di Dewan Rakyat, iaitu kurang 18 kerusi daripada mencapai kadar 1/3 (74 kerusi) yang diminta.
Karim berkata pemimpin-pemimpin terdahulu mengetepikan isu itu dengan alasan bahawa aturan berkenaan tidak pernah ditulis secara rasmi atau dinyatakan secara khusus dalam Perlembagaan.

"Terima kasih, Anwar, kerana dapat memahami perkara yang tidak dapat dilihat, atau memilih untuk tidak dilihat, oleh ramai Ahli Parlimen dari Malaysia Barat serta perdana menteri sebelum ini," katanya.
f0cb17debba475e7: NEW DELHI: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi on Friday for an 11-member BRICS summit where the Middle East conflict will be high on the agenda, Indian broadcasters showed.
Pezeshkian, on his first visit to India as leader, will hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the IRNA news agency said.
The two-day BRICS summit opens on Saturday.

f4fcb81bdcff3df2: PETALING JAYA: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is expected to announce an interim payment for Sarawak’s longstanding claims during the Malaysia Day celebrations in Kuching on Sept 16.
Anwar said he would hold further discussions with Sarawak premier Abang Johari Openg over the next few days to refine the matter, Borneo Post reported.
“Although Sarawak is not covered under Article 112D of the Federal Constitution, I believe the same spirit should be taken into consideration.

“So, I will continue discussions with the premier over the next few days. Hopefully, on Malaysia Day on Sept 16 in Kuching, I can also announce an interim payment for Sarawak,” he told a press conference after chairing the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) implementation action council meeting in Kota Kinabalu today.
In May, Anwar said the interim allocation of RM600 million to Sabah will be increased to RM1.5 billion, pending the finalisation of the state’s constitutional claim to a 40% revenue entitlement.
Sarawak does not have a specific “40% net revenue” clause written into the constitution, and Anwar said Sarawak had proposed introducing a formula to determine the payment.
“Sarawak has also put forward its views on the formula that should be introduced so that it is clear,” he said.
“The formula will take into account the country’s financial position, capacity, as well as the minimum and maximum amounts that can be considered.
“I agree and have instructed the finance ministry and Sarawak government to discuss the introduction of such a formula.”
Abang Johari welcomed the discussions, particularly the decision to determine the formula.
“The formula will be a ‘win-win’ for Sarawak and the federal government,” he said.

3e9a7a18344c8d9c: TORONTO: Toronto rolled out the red carpet for movie stars on Thursday as North America's biggest annual film festival opened with a program of nearly 300 films on topics ranging from political activism to sports.
The Toronto International Film Festival began with the premiere of Apple TV drama "Being Heumann," starring Ruth Madeley as US activist Judy Heumann, who fought for disability rights in the 1970s.
The film deals with "what happens when people refuse to be invisible," said Oscar-winning director Sian Heder at the Princess of Wales Theatre.
"I think that we are living in a time when a lot of groups of people are being left behind," the filmmaker said.
"There are so many battles on so many fronts, and it's hard to know how and where to fight, but collective action matters."
On the red carpet, Heder told AFP that the current situation in the US was part of her motivation for making the film.
"It's like we're rolling back the rights that we fought for in the 1970s at a speed that is just mindblowing. So it is exactly the time for this movie," she said.
Festival CEO Cameron Bailey kicked off the 51st edition with a nod to political tensions between Canada and the US.
Bailey drew applause when he referred to Lake Ontario, which US President Donald Trump had decreed to be renamed "Lake America."
He also emphasized the strength of the Canadian film industry at a time when Trump is championing movies made in the US.
Ten days of film
Highlights in the 293-film program included historical drama "The Housewife," with stars Naomi Watts and Luke Evans attending the premiere on Thursday.
Also in the spotlight were former soccer player Megan Rapinoe, presenting her documentary "Rapinoe," and Jodie Comer and Harry Melling, co-stars of the horror film "Stuffed."
Stars such as John Malkovich, Penelope Cruz, Tom Hiddleston and K-pop phenomenon Lisa are expected to join the festival in the coming days.
Stories of perseverance and unlikely winners are at the heart of the festival's lineup, which will include the premiere of "I Play Rocky."
The film by Oscar-winning director Peter Farrelly tells the improbable story of how Sylvester Stallone went up against Hollywood to produce the breakout movie that would change his life.
Another debuting biopic is "Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend," which recounts the rise of racing star Gilles Villeneuve from his humble beginnings in Quebec to the top of F1.
K-pop superstar Lisa is also set to release her documentary "Always Lalisa," directed by Sue Kim.
Diverse lineup

American comedian and actor Chris Rock will arrive with "Misty Green," the Hollywood satire that marks his return behind the camera, featuring Rosalind Eleazar as a washed-up actress looking for a second chance.
Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, Topher Grace and Rock himself are part of the cast.
Helen Mirren will appear in psychological thriller "A Talent for Murder," directed by Anton Corbijn.
Zack Snyder, director of "300" and "Watchmen," will present "The Last Photograph," which blends drama and action in a mission set in a South American jungle.
Other standouts include "Wild Horse Nine," about two CIA agents on Easter Island during the tense final stretch of Salvador Allende's government in Chile.
The Toronto International Film Festival wraps up on Sept 20.
